title: Gallaty's band, odd jobs, the blues and 'not from Africa'
summary: He describes Bill Gallaty's band members, his picture-show and excursion boat work, and argues that blues and his tunes derive from white sources, not Africa.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: Now, you wanted to ask me about the band that played in Bill Gallaty's band? This man could have been around my age, if he was living today, maybe a year too older than me. He may be the father of some of these Gallaty boys playing around today. That I don't know, because I have never met any of these boys. But they played in the downtown section. Bill Gallaty was the leader, or the manager of the band. And he played valve trombone. They had a boy by the name of Tots, I don't know his right name, played drums. Bull Wendler played the bass violin. And a fellow named by the name of Palaszczuk played clarinet, played clarinet, and I played the clarinet. I followed a boy in there by the name of a Dykeman or something like on that order, who played with him prior to me coming into his band. That is, I took odd jobs with him. I wasn't a regular member of any band. I played on the picture shows. Between 1912 and 14 or 13, I played on the picture shows. I played on the JS Excursion Boat. I was hired there as an extra man. And I played the St. Louis blues, then known to me as Jogo blues, without the middle strain in it. And I had played blues similar to that before I ever heard the St. Louis blues. In my early training at school, at the closing exercise, they had a number they called the Holy City. Well, I had learned this number. And during the, Mr. Sokola was the man who taught us how to go through our little parts in the play. And the whole group was singing. I was in the back singing, and I was making contra melody to this tune. And he called me out in front, and he says, I want you to sing this. And I got out there, and I was stage fright, and I couldn't sing a thing. I couldn't remember what I did. But he thought I did something great, that it would sound good if I would come out in the front and do it. Now, that is, that court construction is not from Africa. That is the court construction, Shorten is the court construction of all the blues. I'll give you an idea how it goes, and let the Negroes, or let these white, excuse me, I was going to say something that's very bad, and I just want to correct myself. These white men that know so much about this music. Tear it to pieces. Tear it to pieces. Tear it to pieces. Tear it to pieces. And so on. Then later come. Tear it to pieces. Da Then comes the other blues that I played and every one of them will fit that chord and not one of them came from Africa like they say this blue chord construction came from. It was camouflaged like I did all my numbers. When I played a tune, if I played a melody and when we come down to what we call a breakdown because of the finger and become difficult to me on the connect I couldn't play that melody and find it in the same place and not being a very versatile musician I had to fake whatever I could come to my ear that I know it come easy with my finger because I'm a faker he has his fingers and his mind that coordinates. Now many of the tunes that I compose are the same way. The last part of the Tiger Rag is nothing but John Philip Souser's March. Da on the horn. I began to say, well, that's good. A faker that you don't know how to play. Now I make That's not Negro music.
